desc:
You are given two arrays of the same length. nums[i] is a number you may change, and cost[i] is the price of changing it by exactly 1 (up or down). Changing nums[i] by d units costs d * cost[i] for that element.

Make all elements of nums equal and return the minimum total cost.

For example, nums = [2, 6, 4] with cost = [1, 1, 5] gives 4: make everything equal to 4 by changing 2 up by 2 (cost 2) and 6 down by 2 (cost 2). And nums = [1, 10] with cost = [3, 1] gives 9: change the cheap element 10 to 1.
hints: For a fixed target t the total cost is sum cost[i] * |nums[i] - t|. Only the target matters now.
This function of t is convex and piecewise linear, with breakpoints at the values of nums. So an optimal t can always be chosen among the values in nums.
It behaves like the median where element i counts cost[i] times. Sort by value and walk until the cumulative weight reaches at least half of the total weight; that value is an optimal target.
editorial: If every cost were 1 the optimum would be the median. With weights, imagine each element repeated cost[i] times; then the weighted median of the multiset is optimal. Moving the target right by one unit changes the cost by (weight of elements left of or at the target) minus (weight of elements right of it), so the cost stops decreasing when the left weight reaches half of the total.

Sort the pairs by nums, accumulate weights until the prefix sum is at least (total + 1) // 2, and take that value as the target. Then sum cost[i] * |nums[i] - target|. Sorting makes it O(n log n). The result is at most about 5,000 * 100 * 500 = 2.5 * 108, safely inside 32-bit integers.
